magnanimous

mag-NAN-uh-muhs · adjective

Hear It

What It Means

Magnanimous is very generous or forgiving, especially toward a rival or someone with less power.

The outgoing mayor was magnanimous during the concession speech, thanking the voters who had chosen someone else.

Example

Though he'd caught his rival cheating on the exam, the magnanimous student chose to warn him privately instead of reporting him.

He had every right to be harsh, but chose generosity and forgiveness instead, which is exactly the quality magnanimous names.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

big-hearted: Big-hearted is warm, giving kindness as someone's everyday nature -- the neighbor who lends anything and forgives easily, whoever asks. Magnanimous is narrower and grander: generosity shown from a position of strength, by the winner toward the defeated or the powerful toward the weak.

noble: Noble covers the whole family of fine, high-minded qualities -- courage, honesty, dignity, and generosity alike. Magnanimous names one specific noble move: rising above the chance to gloat or punish, and treating a beaten rival or a weaker party with striking generosity instead.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

petty: overly concerned with unimportant matters, in a mean-spirited way

vindictive: having a strong desire for revenge

Where it sits · how much you give up for others

polite → magnanimous → self-sacrificing

polite vs. magnanimous: Polite is a weaker virtue than magnanimous: politeness is simply good manners, while a magnanimous winner goes further, showing striking generosity even toward a defeated rival.

self-sacrificing vs. magnanimous: Self-sacrificing goes further than magnanimous: a magnanimous person is generous toward a rival, but a self-sacrificing one is more extreme, giving up their own interests entirely for others.

Build the Word

The pieces

root — magn-: great (also seen in magnitude and magnify) (Latin magnus)

root — anim-: mind, spirit, soul (Latin animus)

suffix — -ous: possessing the quality of (Latin)

Put it together: Magnanimous joins Latin magnus ('great') and animus ('mind, spirit') plus -ous, 'full of' -- literally 'full of great-spiritedness.' A magnanimous person has a spirit too great to be small or petty, even in victory.

Use the root in a new word: magnitude: The report's first page gave the earthquake's magnitude and nothing else.
